name: Bluish charcoal
lede: Bluish charcoal is a dark, muted teal from Japan's traditional color list, measured at the same hex as our library's [[dark-spruce]].

sections.title: In Japan: Kōrainando
sections.body: The name is written 高麗納戸, romanized Kōrainando, which reads literally as "Goryeo storeroom," listed among Japan's traditional colors [1]. *Nando*, storeroom, names a family of muted, low-saturation colors in Japanese tradition; what tied this particular dark teal to Goryeo-era Korea specifically is undocumented in the sources we have [1]. Our library's [[dark-spruce]] sits at the identical measured hex [2]. Further out, [[pale-gunmetal]] and [[outer-space-crayola|Outer Space]] sit in the same small cluster [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds a match for Bluish charcoal in 339 of 23,781 paintings, about 1.4 percent, more common than 69 percent of the named colors we track [3]. It peaks in the 1400s, in 23 of 945 paintings, 2.5 times the rate expected from that century's share of the archive [3]. Inside a painting it is usually hidden rather than prominent, by lightness rank, in 36 percent of its appearances [3]. Paul Cezanne used it most: 7 of his 50 paintings here carry it, 6.0 times his peers' rate [3]. The earliest archive match dates to 1265, and our sources give no Western first-recorded date for this traditional Japanese name to compare it against [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, read as screen colors, not pigment identifications[3].
